fields.name: hp
fields.label: Pump motor size
fields.hint: From the motor nameplate. Most home donkey pumps are half to one hp; submersible and tubewell pumps are larger.

fields.name: other_w
fields.label: Other load running with the pump
fields.hint: Lights and fans that run with the pump. Leave zero if the generator runs the pump alone.

fields.name: other_start_w
fields.label: Starting watts of the other load
fields.hint: Only if the other load has a motor of its own (a fridge or a second pump). Leave blank for lights and fans.

fields.name: motor_eff
fields.label: Motor efficiency
fields.hint: As a decimal. Small single-phase pump motors are about this efficient; a newer motor may be a little better.

fields.name: start_factor
fields.label: Starting surge factor
fields.hint: How many times its running watts the pump draws while starting. Leave blank for the default motor value; a soft starter or VFD lowers it.

fields.name: margin
fields.label: Safety margin on running load
fields.hint: Keeps the generator below full load so it lasts. A decimal like one point two five.

fields.name: pf
fields.label: Generator power factor
fields.hint: Generators are rated in kVA at this power factor. Leave the default unless the nameplate says otherwise.

answer: A {{in.hp|2}} hp well pump draws about {{out.pump_run_w|int}} W while running and about {{out.pump_start_w|int}} W for a second or two while it starts. That surge needs about {{out.recommended_kva|up2}} kVA, so the generator to buy is the next standard size, {{out.standard_kva|1}} kVA. Generator kVA = the larger of running watts × margin or starting watts, ÷ power factor ÷ 1,000.
how: {{in.hp|2}} hp × {{d.w_per_hp|1}} W per hp ÷ {{out.motor_eff|pct}} motor efficiency = {{out.pump_run_w|int}} W running. × {{out.start_factor}} start factor = {{out.pump_start_w|int}} W starting. Other loads add {{out.other_w}} W, so the total is {{out.running_w|int}} W running and {{out.peak_w|int}} W at the moment of starting. The larger of {{out.running_w|int}} W × {{out.margin|2}} margin and {{out.peak_w|int}} W is {{out.sized_w|int}} W; ÷ {{out.pf|2}} power factor ÷ 1,000 = {{out.recommended_kva|up2}} kVA, rounded up to the next standard size, {{out.standard_kva|1}} kVA.
key_facts: A {{in.hp|2}} hp water pump needs about {{out.pump_run_w|int}} W of electrical input while running ({{in.hp|2}} hp × {{d.w_per_hp|1}} W ÷ {{d.motor_eff|pct}} motor efficiency) and about {{out.pump_start_w|int}} W while starting.
Generator size in kVA = the larger of (running watts × {{d.margin|2}}) or (starting watts) ÷ {{d.pf_generator|2}} power factor ÷ 1,000, rounded up to the next standard generator size.
A pump motor draws about {{d.start_factors.motor|int}} times its running watts for a second or two when it starts, and that starting surge, not the running watts, usually decides the generator size.

A {{in.hp|2}} hp pump alone needs a {{out.standard_kva|1}} kVA generator; that size has almost nothing to spare, so with {{ex.3.in.other_w|int}} W of lights and a fan running as well it moves up to {{ex.3.out.standard_kva|1}} kVA, because the pump's start comes on top of everything already on.

formula.text: P_run = hp × 745.7 ÷ η; P_start = P_run × k; kVA = max(P_run × m, P_start) ÷ PF ÷ 1000
lines: hp = motor size in horsepower; 745.7 W per hp
η = motor efficiency (default from the assumptions)
k = starting surge factor for a motor
m = safety margin on the running load
kVA = generator size; the result is rounded up to the next standard size

sections.h2: What size generator do I need to run a water motor?
p: Pick the motor size in hp from the pump nameplate, add any lights or fans that will run at the same time, and the calculator gives the generator size in kVA. A {{in.hp|2}} hp motor is the most common home size and needs a {{out.standard_kva|1}} kVA generator on its own.

The number that matters is the starting surge. A pump motor pulls about {{d.start_factors.motor|int}} times its running watts for a second or two as the rotor comes up to speed. A generator that is only big enough for the running watts will stall, trip or burn its windings every time the pump starts, so the sizing uses the starting watts whenever they are the larger number.

sections.h2: Why are pump starting watts so much higher than running watts?
p: An induction motor at standstill is close to a short circuit until it spins up. The current it draws in that moment is several times the running current; the default here is {{d.start_factors.motor|int}} times, which suits a direct-on-line single-phase pump. Submersible pumps starting against a full column of water can be at the high end of that range.

If your pump has a soft starter or a variable frequency drive, the surge is much smaller and you can lower the starting factor in the advanced options. Only do this if you are sure the pump has one; most Pakistani donkey pumps and submersibles start direct-on-line.

sections.h2: Generator for a submersible pump or tubewell
p: The same formula applies, but submersible and tubewell motors are larger. A {{ex.1.in.hp|2}} hp submersible with {{ex.1.in.other_w|int}} W of lights running needs a {{ex.1.out.standard_kva|1}} kVA generator, and a {{ex.2.in.hp|2}} hp tubewell pump needs {{ex.2.out.standard_kva|1}} kVA on its own because its starting surge is about {{ex.2.out.pump_start_w|int}} W.

A pump whose start needs more than the largest set listed here, {{d.standard_generator_kva.11|int}} kVA, gets no standard size. For such a pump the calculator reports the kVA but no standard size, and a three-phase generator with a soft starter is the usual answer; have an engineer size it.

sections.h2: Generator size for a well pump: standard sizes and the margin
p: Generators are sold in kVA at a power factor of {{d.pf_generator|2}}, so the watts are divided by {{d.pf_generator|2}} to get kVA. The calculated minimum for the {{in.hp|2}} hp pump is {{out.recommended_kva|up2}} kVA, and the next size sold is {{out.standard_kva|1}} kVA. The {{d.margin|2}} margin on the running load keeps the engine from running flat out, which matters for fuel use and engine life.
The kVA needed does not change with supply voltage, so the result is the same for a {{d.v_1ph|int}} V pump in Pakistan and a {{d.v_1ph_us|int}} V pump in North America; only the amps differ.

mistakes: Sizing for the running watts only. The pump starts at about {{d.start_factors.motor|int}} times its running watts, and a generator that cannot supply that surge stalls or trips every time the pump starts.
Treating hp as electrical watts. One hp is {{d.w_per_hp|1}} W of shaft output; the motor draws more from the generator because of its efficiency.
Reading kVA as kW. A generator rated in kVA delivers only {{d.pf_generator|pct}} of that number in watts at the nameplate power factor.
Running the generator at full load. The {{d.margin|2}} margin on the running load is there for engine life and for the fridge or lights someone switches on while the pump runs.

Starting two motors together. If a second pump or a fridge compressor can start at the same moment, enter its starting watts under the other load; the calculator otherwise assumes only the pump starts at once.
safety: Earth the generator, connect it to the house through a proper changeover switch so it can never back-feed the grid, and have a licensed electrician do the wiring.

faq.q: What size generator do I need for a {{ex.0.in.hp|2}} hp water pump?
faq.a: A {{ex.0.in.hp|2}} hp pump draws about {{ex.0.out.pump_run_w|int}} W running and {{ex.0.out.pump_start_w|int}} W starting, so it needs a {{ex.0.out.standard_kva|1}} kVA generator. With {{ex.3.in.other_w|int}} W of lights and a fan on as well it needs {{ex.3.out.standard_kva|1}} kVA, so enter what else runs with the pump.

faq.q: What size generator runs a {{ex.4.in.hp|2}} hp pump?
faq.a: About {{ex.4.out.recommended_kva|up2}} kVA calculated, so a {{ex.4.out.standard_kva|1}} kVA generator. The pump runs at {{ex.4.out.pump_run_w|int}} W but starts at about {{ex.4.out.pump_start_w|int}} W, and the starting surge sets the size.

faq.q: How many kVA are required for a submersible pump?
faq.a: Use the hp on the motor nameplate. A {{ex.1.in.hp|2}} hp submersible needs about {{ex.1.out.standard_kva|1}} kVA with a few lights running, and a {{ex.2.in.hp|2}} hp tubewell pump about {{ex.2.out.standard_kva|1}} kVA. Deep submersibles that start against a full column of water can need the higher end, so do not cut the margin.

faq.q: What are the starting watts of a water pump?
faq.a: About {{d.start_factors.motor|int}} times the running watts for a direct-on-line motor. A {{in.hp|2}} hp pump that runs at {{out.pump_run_w|int}} W starts at about {{out.pump_start_w|int}} W. A soft starter or VFD cuts this a lot.

faq.q: Can a small generator run a well pump if I start it with nothing else on?
faq.a: Only if it can supply the starting surge on top of whatever else is running. Switching the lights and fans off before you start the pump lowers that peak, and on a set sized close to the pump that can decide whether it starts. A generator below the calculated kVA will stall or trip when the pump starts.

faq.q: Is the generator size different at {{d.v_1ph_us|int}} V or {{d.v_1ph|int}} V?
faq.a: No. Watts and kVA are the same at any voltage; only the amps change. Make sure the generator outlet voltage and frequency match the pump motor nameplate.

faq.q: Does the generator size for a well pump change with the depth of the well?
faq.a: Not directly. Depth and flow decide which motor hp the pump needs, and the hp decides the generator. A deeper well usually means a larger motor, which is why submersible pumps tend to need bigger generators than surface donkey pumps.
